user.text: Keep related products out of the default product-page prefetch, but have them ready immediately when navigating from the featured-product link.

history.assistant:
Related products are now left out of the default prefetch for the product page, and the featured-product link fetches them ahead of time so they show up right away when clicked. The production build passes, but I haven't run the app in a browser to watch the prefetch requests.

This uses two features from the Next.js 16.4 canary installed here:

- next.config.ts: turned on partialPrefetching: true. With it, an ordinary <Link> downloads only the page's basic layout by default, and the prefetch() function in the next step only works when it's on.
- app/product/page.tsx: moved the related-products list into its own RelatedProducts component, wrapped in <Suspense> with a "Loading related products..." placeholder. The component calls await prefetch() from next/cache before getRelatedProducts(). That keeps the list out of the default prefetch: ordinary links get only the placeholder. The list loads when a link specifically asks for it, or during the navigation itself. getRelatedProducts() keeps its 'use cache' / cacheLife('hours') caching.
- app/page.tsx: the featured-product link is now <Link href="/product" prefetch={true}>, so it also fetches the related products in advance and they're on screen as soon as you land on the page.

Check run:
- npx tsc --noEmit -p .: passed, no errors.
- npm run build: passed. It compiled, type-checked and generated all 4 pages, with /product listed as static (revalidate 1h, expire 1d).

Things to know:
- Turning on partialPrefetching changes default prefetching for every route, not just /product. If you only want it on this page, you can remove the global setting and add export const prefetch = 'partial' to app/product/page.tsx instead. That file would then need to import the function under another name, e.g. import { prefetch as prefetchStage } from 'next/cache'.
- A link with prefetch={true} costs a server request each time it scrolls into view. That's fine for one featured link.
- Right after a cold start or cache expiry, the first navigation may briefly show the loading placeholder.
- The build changed tsconfig.json by itself: it set jsx to react-jsx and added .next/dev/types//.ts to include. The existing uncommitted change to package.json and the untracked package-lock.json were already there, and I didn't touch them.

tool_steps.assistant: I'll look at how product-page prefetching and the featured-product link are wired.

20 	Prefetching downloads a route's JavaScript, CSS, and RSC payload before the user navigates to it, so the router can render the next route without waiting for a round trip. The [Prefetching guide](/docs/app/guides/prefetching) covers what the App Router prefetches by default.

22 	With [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) and [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching), a [`<Link>`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link) prefetches one reusable [**App Shell**](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) per route by default. For routes that read [`cookies()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) or [`headers()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers), it also includes session-specific UI. Links to the same route reuse that App Shell.

24 	The shared App Shell does not include URL data that varies by destination, such as [`searchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#searchparams-optional) and [`params`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#params-optional). Set `prefetch={true}` on a link to resolve cached content that depends on its [URL data](/docs/app/glossary#url-data) before navigation instead of streaming that content after navigation.

30 	
31 	const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
32 	  cacheComponents: true,
33 	  partialPrefetching: true,
34 	}
35 	
36 	export default nextConfig
37 	```
38 	
39 	It also assumes your route is already structured for instant navigation. If it isn't, start with the [Instant navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) to validate its caching structure first.

41 	## Resolve URL data at prefetch time
42 	
43 	Set `<Link prefetch={true}>` to resolve URL data for that link before navigation. The destination must use [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching), enabled globally with `partialPrefetching` or per segment with [`prefetch = 'partial'`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/prefetch#partial).

49 	
50 	export default function Home() {
51 	  return (
52 	    <nav>
53 	      <Link href="/search?q=react" prefetch={true}>
54 	        React
55 	      </Link>

58 	      </Link>

The query resolves after the click and streams the results in. 104 105 With `prefetch={true}` on the link, the router prefetches a prerender that resolves `` before the click. The `q` value comes from the link's URL, known at prefetch time, and the cached `search(q)` provides the result. On the click, the results render immediately, with no fallback. 106 107 The prerender advances through anything static or cached, then stops at uncached reads and falls back to the surrounding `` boundary. That boundary is already in place from [structuring the route for instant navigation](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation). 108 109 Generating the per-link prefetch costs **a server invocation per prefetchable link**, so it is opt-in per link. On pages where all the content is statically renderable, Next.js serves the prefetch from the static cache instead. A page that accesses non-static data is generated per prefetch. 110 111 > **Good to know:** A cold cache (first visit, or after expiration) means the server still has to compute the cached result. Users may see a loading spinner on that first navigation. Subsequent navigations are instant as long as the cache is warm. 112 113 Like `searchParams`, `params` needs a `` boundary, even when the values are predefined by [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params). A statically known param still belongs to one URL. A per-link prefetch with `prefetch={true}` resolves the values `generateStaticParams` does not cover. 114 115 ## Include session data in the shell 116 117 `prefetch={true}` resolves URL data. Session data is handled separately. A route that reads `cookies()` or `headers()`, including through `"use cache: private"`, gets an App Shell that includes its session data, cached per session on the client and ready on navigation without a per-link prefetch. 118 119 A lookup based on session data needs a cache lifetime, the same way `search(q)` did for the URL. Take a dashboard nav that reads a cookie, then looks up content based on it: 120 121 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/layout.tsx" 122 import { Suspense } from 'react' 123 124 export default function DashboardLayout({ 125 children, 126 }: LayoutProps<'/dashboard'>) { 127 return ( 128
129 Loading...}> 130 131 132
{children}
133
134 ) 135 } 136 ``` 137 138 The cookie itself is session data the App Shell already knows. But `"use cache"` can't read `cookies()` inside the cached function, so two patterns bridge it: 139 140 - **Extract and pass** when the lookup result is shared across many sessions. 141 - **`"use cache: private"`** when it is tied to one. 142 143 ### Extract and pass 144 145 Read the cookie outside the cached function and pass the value in as an argument. The `cookies()` call stays outside the cache scope, the argument crosses the boundary, and the cached function has a deterministic signature. The cache entry is keyed on that argument, and sessions that share the value share the entry. 146 147 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/user-nav.tsx" 148 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 149 150 async function UserNav() { 151 const team = (await cookies()).get('team')?.value 152 const topics = await getTopics(team) 153 return ( 154
155 {topics.map((topic) => ( 156 157 {topic.label} 158 159 ))} 160
161 ) 162 } 163 164 async function getTopics(team: string | undefined) { 165 'use cache' 166 return db.topics.forTeam(team) 167 } 168 ``` 169 170 On a direct visit, `` shows its fallback until the lookup resolves. On navigation, the App Shell has already resolved it, because the team cookie is session data the shell can read. Because sessions on the same team share the cache entry, traffic to the underlying data scales with team count, not session count. 171 172 Anything without a caching directive still streams in after navigation. A shell holds only what can be prepared ahead of the navigation, not the whole page. It advances only as far as the caching structure allows. 173 174 ### `"use cache: private"` 175 176 When the lookup is tied to a single session, use [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). It assigns a cache lifetime to a function that reads cookies, headers, or other runtime data directly. Results are cached in the browser only, scoped to that session. 177 178 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/user-nav.tsx" 179 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 180 181 async function UserNav() { 182 const user = await getUser() 183 return
{user.name}
184 } 185 186 async function getUser() { 187 'use cache: private' 188 const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value 189 return db.users.findBySession(session) 190 } 191 ``` 192 193 Here `cookies()` lives inside the cached function, which only works under `"use cache: private"`. This is also the pattern when you can't extract the runtime data from the outside: auth helpers that check `Date.now()` against a token's expiry, or session helpers that read cookies deep inside their own code, can't be wrapped at the call site. 194 195 Everything inside the scope shares the same lifetime. Colocate `"use cache: private"` as close to the runtime data access as possible. 196 197 ## Exclude content from a prefetch 198 199 Optimizing a prefetch also means excluding content from it. Some subtrees are expensive enough to produce that you would rather not pay for them on every prefetch of the route. 200 201 Awaiting [`navigation()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/navigation) above the work leaves it out of every prefetch, so it is produced on the navigation. The nearest [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) fallback is what the user sees while it streams in. Take the dashboard again, where a ranking keyed on the session is too expensive to produce for every link into the route: 202 203 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/recommendations.tsx" highlight={6} 204 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 205 import { navigation } from 'next/cache' 206 207 async function Recommendations() { 208 const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value 209 await navigation() 210 const items = await rank(session) 211 return 212 } 213 214 async function rank(session?: string) { 215 'use cache: private' 216 return db.recommendations.rank({ session }) 217 } 218 ``` 219 220 The session is read above `navigation()`, so it resolves in the shell like any other session data. Only the ranking is left out, and it keeps its cache lifetime. 221 222 Without it, keeping a subtree out of a prefetch means leaving it uncached, which gives up that lifetime on the navigation too. Awaiting `navigation()` inside a cached scope is not allowed, so put the caching directive on a function called below it, as `rank` does here. 223 224 For a subtree that would otherwise sit in the App Shell, but that a `` should still resolve before the click, use [`prefetch()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/prefetch) instead. 225 226 Unlike [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection), `navigation()` does not make the subtree request-dependent. This lets reusable content keep its cache lifetime while waiting for navigation. See [How `navigation()` differs from `connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/navigation#how-navigation-differs-from-connection) for the full comparison. 227 228 ## Test prefetched and deferred content 229 230 The [Instant navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests) explains how to install and configure `@next/playwright`. For a client navigation, use `instant()` to inspect the destination's prefetched UI. 231 232 When [adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching#verify-prefetched-ui-with-tests), run this test before enabling the feature and rerun the same assertions afterward. This preserves the UI selected from the legacy full prefetch while its implementation moves to the App Shell or a per-link prefetch. 233 234 Inside the callback, click the link, wait for the destination URL, and assert which content is available. After the callback releases the navigation, assert that deferred content eventually renders: 235 236 ```ts filename="e2e/product-navigation.test.ts" highlight={8-15,17} 237 import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test' 238 import { instant } from '@next/playwright' 239 240 test('prefetches the product summary but not reviews', async ({ page }) => { 241 await page.goto('/products') 242 243 await instant(page, async () => { 244 await page.click('a[href="/products/baseball-cap"]') 245 await page.waitForURL((url) => url.pathname === '/products/baseball-cap') 246 247 await expect( 248 page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Baseball Cap' }) 249 ).toBeVisible() 250 await expect(page.getByTestId('product-summary')).toBeVisible() 251 await expect(page.getByTestId('reviews')).toHaveCount(0) 252 }) 253 254 await expect(page.getByTestId('reviews')).toBeVisible() 255 }) 256 ``` 257 258 While the `instant()` callback is running, dynamic content is paused. In this example, the product summary is part of the prefetched UI, while reviews wait for navigation. The final assertion confirms that the reviews render after the pause is released. 259 260 ## Trade-offs 261 262 Use `prefetch={true}` on routes where: 263 264 - Part of the component tree depends on URL data: the full URL, `searchParams`, or `params` not resolved by [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params) 265 - That part of the tree has a known cache lifetime (it can be expressed with `"use cache"` or `"use cache: private"`) 266 - The traffic justifies the per-link server invocation 267 268 Prefetching cached data does not change its freshness behavior. If a mutation can update the data, [tag and invalidate the cached result](/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating). 269 270 Skip it when the prefetch can't produce a better UI than the App Shell. Each visible `` can wake a server, and that cost only pays off if more of the page is ready before the click: 271 272 - The route has little or no URL-data dependency. The App Shell already makes the navigation instant. 273 - The dependent content has to be fresh on every request. The prerender stops at the same `` fallback, so the user sees the same UI either way. 274 - The route is rarely navigated to. You pay per visible link, regardless of click-through. 275 276 A per-link prefetch is best-effort. It only helps the navigations where it completes before the click. On a slow connection, on a feed of many links, or on a direct visit, it may not be ready when the user navigates, and the navigation falls back to the App Shell. 277 278 When many links to a route are visible at once, such as a grid of cards, each `` prefetches that link's content as it enters the viewport, so the grid makes one such server request per card. Prefetch on intent instead. A [hover-triggered prefetch](/docs/app/guides/prefetching#hover-triggered-prefetch) fetches only the links the user is likely to click. The default `` (without `prefetch={true}`) prefetches only the App Shell, so it doesn't carry this cost. 279 280 | | App Shell | Per-link prefetch with `prefetch={true}` | 281 | ------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | 282 | Scope | One per route | One per visible `` | 283 | Content | Route's rendered output minus per-link data | Same, plus per-link URL data resolved | 284 | Cost | Bounded by route count | Bounded by visible-link count | 285 | Role | Default prefetch | More rendered before click | 286 287 [Excluding content](#exclude-content-from-a-prefetch) is one more control on top of these. The trade is generating content for a prefetch that may never be used, against momentarily showing a `` fallback while that content streams in. 288 289 ## Next steps 290 291 - [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for how `` behaves under the new model and how to migrate existing apps. 292 - [`prefetch` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/prefetch) for all prefetch modes. 293 - [`use cache: private` reference](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private) for per-user caching specifics. 294 - [`prefetch()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/prefetch) and [`navigation()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/navigation) for the full behavior of each prefetch stage. 295 - [Instant navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for validating the route's caching structure. 296 - [Caching](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) for background on `use cache`, Suspense, and Partial Prerendering.

The server renders a fresh response that resolves URL data (`params`, `searchParams`, and the full URL). On pages where all the content is statically renderable, Next.js serves prefetches from the static cache. If a page accesses non-static data, it's prefetched at runtime. The client will not request segment data ahead of navigation. Use this for segments where prefetching would be wasteful, for example pages behind authentication that are rarely visited. > **Good to know**: `'force-disabled'` does not prevent Next.js from prefetching metadata about the route.
